section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Bernoulli Trial
section_1.content: Introduce the simplest building block of probability: a single event with only two outcomes (Success or Failure). Explain that for a trial to be Bernoulli, the probability of success (p) must remain constant.
section_1.example: Meet 'Pixel the Penguin'. Pixel tries to catch a fish. He either succeeds (Success) or misses (Failure). There is no middle ground. If Pixel has a 60% chance of catching a fish (p=0.6), every single attempt is a Bernoulli trial.

section_2.title: Defining the Binomial Setting (BINS)
section_2.content: Transition from one trial to multiple trials. Introduce the 'BINS' criteria to identify a Binomial Distribution: Binary outcomes, Independent trials, fixed Number of trials (n), and Same probability (p) for each trial.
section_2.example: Pixel the Penguin goes fishing 10 times (n=10). Each attempt is independent (one catch doesn't affect the next), the outcome is always catch/miss, and his skill (p=0.6) stays the same. This 'fishing trip' follows a Binomial Distribution.

section_3.title: The Formula: Breaking Down the Logic
section_3.content: Deconstruct the Binomial Formula: P(X=k) = nCk * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k). Use a visual flow: 1. 'nCk' counts the number of ways/paths to get k successes. 2. 'p^k' is the probability of the successes. 3. '(1-p)^(n-k)' is the probability of the failures.
section_3.example: Visual: A tree diagram showing Pixel catching exactly 2 fish out of 3 tries. The animation highlights three different paths (S-S-F, S-F-S, F-S-S), showing that nCk (3C2) equals 3 possible ways to achieve the result.

section_4.title: Visualizing the Distribution Shape
section_4.content: Show how the distribution looks as a histogram. Explain how changing 'n' (number of trials) and 'p' (probability) alters the center and spread. Highlight the 'Bell Curve' shape that emerges when 'n' is large.
section_4.example: An interactive bar chart showing Pixel's fishing results. When p=0.5, the bars are perfectly symmetrical. When p=0.1 (low skill), the bars pile up on the left (skewed right). As we increase n from 10 to 50, the bars smoothen into a symmetric mountain shape.

section_5.title: Real-World Application & Summary
section_5.content: Summarize the key takeaways: How to identify, calculate, and visualize Binomial events. Briefly mention where this is used in the real world (e.g., quality control, sports stats, or medical trials).
section_5.example: A 'Quality Control Robot' on a factory line checking 100 microchips. If 2% are usually defective (p=0.02), we can use the Binomial Distribution to predict the probability of finding exactly 5 broken chips in a batch, helping the factory manage risk.
